INT. UPSCALE RESTAURANT – EVENING

A quiet hum of conversation and clinking cutlery fills the warm, amber-lit space. At a corner table, ELENA (early 30s, composed, elegant) sips her wine. Across from her sits MARCUS (late 30s, charming, attentive), swirling his own glass with a smile that doesn’t quite reach his eyes.

The waiter places their entrees down with a flourish and retreats.

MARCUS
This place really does live up to the reviews. You always pick the right spot.

ELENA (smiling)
I try. Ambiance is half the meal, don’t you think?

She cuts into her salmon delicately, her posture perfect. Inside, her mind is racing.

He’s too calm. He must suspect something. Don’t let it show. Just keep the rhythm—casual, warm, unreadable.

MARCUS
Still, I’m impressed. It’s rare to meet someone with such precise taste. Makes me wonder what else you’re precise about.

He offers a light chuckle and leans in slightly, eyes fixed on her. He watches her reaction like a hunter studying a breeze.

She’s hiding something. That phone call she silenced earlier—she flinched. Not the kind of flinch that comes from spam. I need more time. Patience. Smile.

ELENA (laughing softly)
Well, I suppose I’m precise about most things. Comes with the job. You can’t exactly negotiate international contracts on instinct.

Redirect. Keep it on the professional. Don’t let him ask about last Thursday. Don’t let him ask about the safe deposit box.

MARCUS
True. But instinct has its place. Sometimes it tells you more than facts ever could.

He takes a sip of wine, his eyes still on her, the statement hanging in the air like a test. Elena meets his gaze evenly, her voice smooth.

ELENA
And sometimes it leads you straight into a trap.

Did that land too hard? No. Good. Keep smiling. He doesn’t know. He couldn’t have seen the file. The lock was untouched.

Marcus laughs, seemingly at ease, but he shifts in his seat.

She’s deflecting. Clever. But if she knew what I found on her laptop, she wouldn’t be sitting so calmly. Unless she thinks I’ll play along. Maybe I will—for now.

MARCUS
Touché. You know, I’ve always admired your confidence. It’s... magnetic.

ELENA
Thank you. Confidence is just practice, really. Like fencing. Or lying.

She tilts her head slightly, as if teasing. He laughs again, louder this time, but his hand tightens around his fork.

That was a message. She knows. Or she thinks she does. She’s bluffing. Or maybe I am. Either way, I can’t move yet. Not until I know who else she’s told.

MARCUS
Well, whatever your secret is, I hope it’s not dangerous. I’d hate to find out I’ve been dining with a femme fatale.

ELENA (smiling sweetly)
And I’d hate to find out I’ve been dining with someone who already knows too much.

For a moment, they hold each other’s gaze, the candlelight flickering between them like a silent metronome. Then, almost simultaneously, they both laugh—light, effortless, practiced.

This is a dance. Only one of us will lead when the music stops. For now, keep twirling.

FADE OUT.

INT. UPSCALE RESTAURANT – EVENING

Soft candlelight glimmers across polished wine glasses. A string quartet plays faintly in the background. Two people sit across from each other at a white-linen table:*

MARGOT, mid-40s, elegant, poised, dressed in navy silk — every movement precise. Opposite her sits THOMAS, early 50s, genial, slightly rumpled in a way that suggests either comfort or carelessness. The food before them is mostly untouched.

They smile politely.

THOMAS
(raising his glass)
To old friends — and new beginnings.

Margot clinks her glass lightly, her smile unwavering.

MARGOT
To looking ahead. And leaving the past where it belongs.

THOMAS
(chuckles)
Amen to that.

They sip. Margot’s eyes linger on Thomas a beat too long. She sets her glass down carefully, her fingers brushing the rim.

MARGOT
You always did enjoy a bit of ceremony. Even back at the firm — remember the quarterly reviews?

THOMAS
(grinning)
Ah, yes. The dreaded PowerPoints and obligatory pastries. I swear, those muffins could have killed someone.

He laughs, but Margot doesn’t. She tilts her head slightly, as if studying him.

MARGOT
Yet you always seemed to thrive under pressure.

THOMAS
What can I say? I learned from the best.

He raises his eyebrows meaningfully. Margot’s smile tightens.

She knows he’s baiting her. He always admired her ambition — until it turned against him. Until she discovered what he buried in those quarterly reports. But he doesn’t know she knows. Not yet.

MARGOT
Flattery, Thomas? I thought we’d moved beyond that.

THOMAS
Just giving credit where it’s due.

He can't afford to let her suspect what he’s planning. Not tonight. Not before the board vote. If she senses his hand in it, she’ll strike first — like she did last time.

A waiter appears, removing their untouched plates. Margot waves him off gently.

MARGOT
I suppose we’re both too distracted to eat.

THOMAS
Just a lot on my mind, that’s all.

MARGOT
Anything I can help with?

Her tone is sweet, but there’s a flicker behind her eyes — a quiet challenge.

THOMAS
That depends. Are we still on the same side?

The question hangs in the air like cigar smoke. Margot sips her wine slowly, never breaking eye contact.

MARGOT
Of course we are. We always want what’s best for the company.

She almost laughs at the lie. But she can’t reveal her hand — not while she’s still gathering proof. The offshore account. The shell contracts. He thinks they’re buried. He doesn’t know she’s already spoken to Audit.

THOMAS
That’s good to hear.

She’s bluffing — he’s sure of it. But even a bluff can be dangerous in her hands. He needs to move faster. The anonymous tip to the press goes out tonight. By morning, her name will be the one in the headlines.

Margot glances at her watch.

MARGOT
Well, this has been… enlightening.

THOMAS
It always is, with you.

They stand. Margot offers her hand. Thomas takes it.

Her grip is firm. Too firm. She knows. Or she suspects. But even if she does, it’s already too late.

His palm is warm. Steady. He believes he’s ahead. But he underestimates how far she’s willing to go.

MARGOT
Good night, Thomas.

THOMAS
Good night, Margot.

They part like old colleagues — with grace and civility. Lovers might kiss. Enemies might glare. But this... this is something colder.

As Margot walks toward the valet, she dials a number on her phone — then pauses.

MARGOT
(into phone)
Yes. Proceed.

Cut to Thomas at the curb, texting quickly.

THOMAS (TEXTING):
Send the file. Now.

FADE OUT.

Scene: A Quiet Dinner at Le Papillon

Setting: A small, softly lit French restaurant in the city. The rain taps gently against the windowpane. A candle flickers between two plates of coq au vin. Across the table sit CLAIRE, in her mid-thirties, composed in a navy blouse, and ADRIAN, early forties, in a tailored charcoal suit. They smile, sip wine, and carefully mind their words.

CLAIRE:
The sauce is wonderful, isn’t it? There’s something about red wine and thyme that makes everything feel warmer.

She swirls her fork through the sauce, her smile practiced. Her left hand is steady, though her pulse flutters at her wrist. The envelope in her purse—marked CLASSIFIED—presses like a stone against her side.

ADRIAN:
Absolutely. It’s comforting. Like something you’d come home to after a long trip.

He holds her gaze a beat longer than necessary, masking the flicker of doubt behind his eyes. He knows she’s not who she says she is. He’s seen the surveillance photos tucked in the folder beneath the floorboards of his study.

CLAIRE:
You travel a lot, don’t you? For work.

She breaks a piece of baguette, her tone casual. But she’s fishing—trying to confirm the schedule she intercepted last week. If he’s lying now, she’ll know.

ADRIAN:
Too much, really. Frankfurt last week, then Geneva. I’m due in Brussels next month.

He lies smoothly. Frankfurt was canceled. Geneva was a detour. Brussels is a trap. He watches her reaction carefully. If she flinches, he’ll have his answer.

CLAIRE:
You must have a fantastic memory to keep it all straight. I can barely remember which meetings I’ve lied my way out of.

She laughs softly, making light of the words. But her stomach knots. He didn’t flinch. Either he’s telling the truth—or he’s better at this than she thought.

ADRIAN:
Selective memory is a gift. I remember the important things.

He sips his wine, letting the silence linger just long enough to suggest something more. He wonders if she remembers Istanbul. The alley. The camera flash. The man who never came home.

CLAIRE:
Important things like birthdays? Or… secrets?

She meets his eyes now, her smile sharper. She’s testing the edge, wondering how close she can step to the line without falling over it.

ADRIAN:
Secrets are only dangerous when they’re shared.

His voice is calm, but his knuckles whiten around the stem of his glass. He recalls the message he decrypted this morning: “The courier is in position. Confirm identity.” He hasn’t confirmed it yet. But he’s close.

CLAIRE:
Then I suppose we’re very safe.

She raises her glass. Her fingers tremble just enough to make the candlelight dance in her wine. She tells herself she won’t hesitate when the time comes. Even if she likes the way he says her name.

ADRIAN:
To safety.

He clinks his glass to hers. He wonders how much she knows. Whether she’s guessed the third agent. Whether she’ll make it out tonight. Whether he wants her to.

They drink. They smile. The rain continues. Two people dining politely, their words laced with elegance, their intentions armed to the teeth.

Scene: A Private Dinner at an Upscale Restaurant

A soft golden glow from the chandelier spills over a well-dressed couple seated at a small, intimate table. Fine crystal glasses catch the light, and the smell of roasted duck and rosemary wafts from the plates. The clink of cutlery and the murmur of other diners form a gentle backdrop.

Characters:

  • Clara, mid-30s, composed, elegant, with an air of practiced ease. She works in acquisitions at a prestigious art museum.
  • Daniel, early 40s, sharp dresser, charming, with an undercurrent of calculation. He’s a private collector and art consultant.

They are sharing a bottle of red wine, both smiling politely.

CLARA (lifting her glass):
To successful collaborations and the thrill of rare discoveries.

DANIEL (touching his glass to hers):
And to trust between allies in the art world.

Clara smiles, but a flicker of tension tightens her jaw. She takes a sip, watching him over the rim of her glass.

CLARA:
It’s not every day a piece like the Vermeer sketch surfaces. You must have been delighted to find it.

DANIEL:
Ecstatic. You know how these things go—half instinct, half luck.
(And a little forgery, but let’s not ruin the mood.)

CLARA:
Hmm. The provenance checks out, at least on paper.
(Which makes it all the more impressive that it’s fake. Who forged it for you, Daniel?)
The museum’s board is intrigued.

DANIEL (smiling):
Intrigue is a good sign. It means they’re interested.

He cuts into his duck, deliberately slow. He’s watching her too, but with the relaxed air of someone used to control.

DANIEL:
And you? Are you convinced?

CLARA (measuring):
I’m…curious.
(And I’m this close to exposing you. But I need more. I need you to slip.)
Tell me again how it came to you?

DANIEL:
A contact in Antwerp. Old estate, dusty attic, the usual romance.
(The details are blurry enough to be believable. She won’t press too hard—she can’t afford to.)
You know how these finds are more about relationships than records.

CLARA:
Oh, absolutely.
(Like the relationship I’ve built with Interpol’s art crimes division.)
It’s all about who you trust.

A beat. They both smile. The waiter refills their glasses.

DANIEL (leaning in slightly):
I trust you, Clara. You’ve got a sharp eye. And discretion.

CLARA:
Thank you. Discretion is…everything in our field.
(Especially when you're feeding intel to bring someone down without tipping your hand.)

DANIEL:
I hope this will be the first of many deals between us.

CLARA:
Let’s see how this one goes first.
(Because if I’m right, your empire’s about to crumble.)

DANIEL (raising an eyebrow):
Fair enough. Patience is a virtue.
(She’s hiding something. Has she seen through the sketch? Or is she fishing?)

CLARA:
In our world, patience is survival.

They both sip their wine. A pause. A smile. A silent war.

DANIEL:
So. Dessert?

CLARA:
Why not?
(The night’s still young, and the truth always finds its way to the surface—eventually.)

Fade out as the waiter returns with menus, and the polite conversation continues—a dance of masks, each waiting for the other to blink first.

Scene: A Quiet Corner of an Upscale Restaurant

The soft clinking of silverware and the gentle hum of conversation fill the air. Candlelight flickers between two wine glasses on a white linen tablecloth. Across from each other sit Evelyn and Marcus, both dressed impeccably, their smiles poised—pleasant, practiced.

EVELYN: (smiling warmly)
This place is lovely, Marcus. You always find the most charming spots.

MARCUS: (returning the smile)
Only the best for you, Evelyn. I remembered you liked French cuisine.

He remembers. Of course he does. He always pays attention to the little things. It would almost be sweet—if he weren’t the reason Paul disappeared.

EVELYN: (tilting her head slightly)
It’s been, what, six months since we last saw each other?

MARCUS:
Seven, I think. Time moves strangely these days. But some things stay the same.

Seven months since I saw you at Paul’s party. The night before he went missing. Seven months of pretending I don’t know more than I let on.

EVELYN: (gently swirling her wine)
And how’s work? Still with the firm?

MARCUS: (nodding)
Yes. Still drowning in contracts and acquisitions. You know how it is.

Still a safe answer. Still the same mask. She doesn’t know. She can’t know about Zurich, or the offshore account. And she definitely doesn’t know what Paul threatened to expose.

EVELYN:
I heard from mutual friends that you’ve been traveling more lately?

MARCUS: (pauses, then chuckles)
Guilty. A few conferences. A little skiing in the Alps. You’d love it there—so serene.

Keep it light. Keep it vague. She’s fishing. But she won't find anything. Not unless she knows where to dig.

EVELYN: (smiling tightly)
Sounds wonderful. You always did know how to disappear for a while.

Like Paul did. But he didn’t leave a forwarding address. And I found the note. The one with your handwriting.

MARCUS: (raising his glass)
To old friends. And to... rediscovering things we thought we lost.

EVELYN: (clinks glasses, her eyes narrowing slightly)
To finding answers.

To making you slip. Because sooner or later, you will.

MARCUS:
You’ve always had a curious mind, Evelyn. That’s what I admire most about you.

EVELYN: (smiles sweetly)
Funny. That’s what Paul said too.

A calculated move. A memory placed like bait. Let’s see if he flinches.

MARCUS: (his smile falters for half a second, then recovers)
He had good taste in people.

And an unfortunate tendency to dig too deep. Just like you. God help me, Evelyn—don’t make me do to you what I had to do to him.

EVELYN: (leaning in slightly, voice soft)
Do you ever think about him?

MARCUS: (holding her gaze)
Every now and then. Some people leave an impression.

You’re not the only one watching, Evelyn. I know you’ve been asking questions. I know you think you’re close. But you’re not. You don’t know what he was into. What I had to clean up.

EVELYN: (sitting back, smile still intact)
Well. Here’s to impressions, then.

MARCUS:
And to the truth—however well we hide it.

And to the game we’re playing. One of us will lose. I just hope it’s not you.

The waiter arrives with the check. Marcus reaches for it. Evelyn doesn’t protest.

Outside, the city pulses with quiet tension. Inside, under candlelight, two smiles linger—sharp as blades beneath velvet.

Scene: A Quiet Dinner at a Seaside Restaurant

Setting: The sun is setting beyond the horizon, painting the sky in hues of coral and lavender. Soft jazz filters through the air. MARISSA and GRAHAM sit across from each other at a corner table by the window, sipping wine and sharing a plate of grilled sea bass. The mood is calm, bordering on intimate. But beneath the surface, both are navigating treacherous waters.

MARISSA (smiling gently):
The sea air always makes food taste better, don’t you think?

GRAHAM (nodding, setting down his fork):
Absolutely. There’s something about salt in the air—it sharpens everything. Makes it real.

—Marissa tilts her head slightly, noting the word “real.” She wonders if he meant that. Real. Like the forged documents hidden in her hotel room, still smelling faintly of ink.

MARISSA:
It does. It brings clarity. I’ve missed this... being away from the city, I mean. Everything feels less complicated here.

GRAHAM (chuckling):
Complication is overrated. Simplicity has its own elegance.

—He smiles, but he’s thinking of the USB drive in his coat pocket. The one with surveillance photos of Marissa crossing the border under a different name. If she knew he knew…

MARISSA (lifting her glass toward him):
To simplicity, then.

GRAHAM (clinking glasses):
To simplicity.

—They sip. Graham watches her over the rim of his glass. She's composed, too composed. Her laugh earlier had come half a second too late. But he can’t move too fast. Not yet.

MARISSA (setting down her glass):
You’ve been... quieter than usual tonight. Everything alright?

GRAHAM (shrugging, easy smile returning):
Just absorbing it all. The food, the view... your company. It’s not every day I get to dine with someone as intriguing as you.

—He leans back, eyes calm. Inside, he’s calculating. If she’s the leak, he needs her to trust him. But if he’s wrong… he pushes that thought aside.

MARISSA (feigning a blush):
That’s very kind of you. I’d say the same, though I suspect you’re hiding your true self behind that charming smile.

GRAHAM (laughing):
Guilty. Aren’t we all?

—Her smile tightens just slightly. Yes, we are, she thinks. She wonders if he’s guessed anything. He hasn’t asked about Berlin, or Prague. He’s too smooth. Too careful.

MARISSA:
I suppose it’s human nature, isn’t it? To wear masks. Even over dinner.

GRAHAM (raising an eyebrow):
Especially over dinner. That’s when the stakes are highest—first impressions, last chances.

—He watches the way her hand hesitates over her fork. A flicker. Almost imperceptible. But he was trained to spot hesitation. To know when someone was lying.

MARISSA (quietly):
And what are the stakes tonight, Graham?

GRAHAM (meeting her gaze):
That depends on what you’re hiding.

—A beat of silence. Their eyes lock. The jazz fades into the background. For a moment, the masks slip—just a fraction. Enough to reveal the glint of steel beneath the silk.

MARISSA (smiling, tilting her head):
Then maybe we should both be careful what we reveal.

—And just like that, the moment passes. The waiter approaches with dessert menus. They smile, thank him, and return to their performance. But the air has changed. The dance has begun.

End Scene.

INT. UPSCALE RESTAURANT – EVENING

A quiet hum of conversation. Crystal glasses clink. Candlelight flickers between two people seated across from each other in a small booth.

ISABELLE, mid-30s, elegant and composed, folds her napkin with delicate precision. Across from her, MARCUS, 40, charming in a tailored blazer, smiles with practiced ease. The table holds half-finished plates of salmon and risotto.

MARCUS
(smiling)
I have to say, Isabelle, this place has excellent taste—for someone who used to eat instant ramen in college.

ISABELLE
(laughs softly)
We all evolve. Though I still miss the simplicity of it. Just hot water and a little patience.

She keeps her tone light, but her eyes flick to his wrist—a glint of something metallic beneath his cuff. A bracelet? Or a tracker? She smiles again, too quickly.

MARCUS
Yes, patience. Something I’ve had to develop lately. Things take time—careful planning, measured steps.

He’s watching her too closely. She stirs her wine, letting the silence stretch an extra beat.

ISABELLE
True. Though sometimes, things happen in a blink. A sudden shift. One moment, you’re living your life, and the next… everything’s changed.

Her voice is calm, but her mind races. Did he pick up the shift schedule? Does he know about the signal buried in the dessert codes?

MARCUS
(chuckling)
Sounds like someone’s been reading too many thrillers.

ISABELLE
Only the ones with unreliable narrators.

They share a laugh. Marcus sips his wine, swirling it once before setting it down. He leans forward slightly.

MARCUS
Tell me something, Isabelle. What drew you to art restoration? It’s such a delicate field—every move matters. One wrong stroke, and the whole piece is ruined.

He’s testing her. She knows it. Her fingers tighten around her fork.

ISABELLE
It’s the intimacy, I suppose. Being close enough to see the fractures... and knowing how to hide them.

His eyes narrow just slightly. She sees it. So he does know. Or suspect. She keeps her breathing steady.

MARCUS
That’s poetic. You always had a way with words.

ISABELLE
Well, words are like paintings. Layers of meaning. You just have to know where to look.

A waiter passes. They both smile politely, pausing until he’s gone. Marcus cuts a piece of fish, his voice casual.

MARCUS
So, you’re heading to Berlin next week?

ISABELLE
Yes. A Rothko restoration. Supposedly minor damage, but... you know how it is. Sometimes the worst cracks are underneath.

Berlin. The drop point. Does he know? Has he intercepted it?

MARCUS
I envy your travel. My work’s kept me grounded lately—lots of paperwork, endless vetting. But it’s rewarding, in its own way.

“Vetting.” She hears the weight of it. Like a net being drawn tight. She offers a wistful smile.

ISABELLE
Rewarding is important. Though sometimes... the cost is buried in the fine print.

A pause. Their eyes meet. The candle flickers between them.

MARCUS
To old friends. And new beginnings.

ISABELLE
(softly)
To masks that fit well enough to forget you’re wearing them.

They clink glasses. Sip. Each watching the other over the rim.

ISABELLE (INTERNAL)
He’s here to confirm it. The agency suspects. But he doesn’t have proof yet. I have to stay calm. Play the part. Just until I reach Berlin.

MARCUS (INTERNAL)
She’s slippery. But the Rothko is the key—she’s passing intel through pigments. I’ll follow her to Berlin. This time, she won’t vanish.

They smile again. A delicate dance, each step precise. The orchestra swells in the background, unaware of the quiet war playing out between candlelight and wine.

Scene: “The Dinner Guest”
Setting: A warmly lit dining room in a quiet suburban home. A long, oak table sits between MARION, a poised woman in her early 60s, and ELIAS, a neatly dressed man in his 30s. The table is elegantly set—linen napkins, polished silverware, a half-empty bottle of wine between them. A roast chicken has been carved, and the remnants of an elaborate meal rest on their plates.

MARION:
You’ve picked up the Pinot quite nicely. Not everyone appreciates the softer Burgundy notes.

She lifts her glass with a gentle smile. She holds it like a practiced hostess, her fingers delicate, hiding the tremor in her wrist.

ELIAS (smiling):
It’s lovely. Reminds me of something I had in Dijon once. When I was... studying abroad.

He swirls his glass. The truth is, he’s never been to France. But he knows enough to sound like he has. Every detail matters. Every lie must be seamless.

MARION:
Dijon, really? How charming. I spent a summer in Arles during my college years. It stays with you. Something about the light.

She watches his eyes carefully. Too carefully. She’s trained herself to read people. For years, she had to. The light in Arles hadn’t stayed with her—what stayed was the sound of her husband’s voice the day he disappeared.

ELIAS:
Yes, the light. Exactly.

He nods, not really sure what she means. He’s not here for the wine or the conversation. He’s here because he believes this woman knows something—about a man named Daniel Carter. His father.

MARION (cutting into her chicken):
You said your parents lived upstate? Somewhere near Hudson?

She already knows this isn’t true. There’s no birth record for Elias Moore in any of the counties he claimed. She’s checked. Twice.

ELIAS (without hesitation):
Yes. My mother still lives there. My father passed a few years ago.

He says it calmly, but his chest tightens. Passed is too soft a word. Vanished is more accurate. Disappeared in 1995—last seen leaving a business meeting in Boston. A meeting Marion attended.

MARION:
I’m sorry to hear that. Loss never quite leaves us, does it?

She speaks with sincerity. But inside, she’s calculating. Could he know? Is he here for answers or vengeance? Her hands are steady now, her pulse measured. She’s been through this before.

ELIAS:
No, it doesn’t. It just... changes shape.

He meets her eyes. He wants to see guilt there. Remorse. But she’s composed, a sculpture of politeness. He wonders if he has the wrong person. Or if she’s simply better at hiding.

MARION (tilting her head):
I’m glad you reached out. I don’t often host former students. What made you think of me?

She already suspects. He was never her student. But she lets the lie sit there, undisturbed, like an old photograph in a drawer.

ELIAS:
You made an impression. Your lectures on moral ambiguity... they stuck with me.

He says it with a faint smile. The irony is rich, and bitter. He wonders if she knows he’s quoting her own book back to her. The one she published just after the investigation closed.

MARION (raising her glass):
To ambiguity, then. May it never outshine clarity.

Her toast is elegant, rehearsed. But her hand brushes the ring on her finger—her husband’s. It’s a prop now. She wears it like a shield.

ELIAS (clinking his glass against hers):
To answers. Wherever they may hide.

Their eyes lock. The clink is soft, but final, like a gavel falling.

Outside, the wind picks up. The curtains flutter slightly. Inside, two people smile across a table, their words gentle, their secrets coiled beneath every syllable—waiting.

Scene: A Quiet Dinner in the City

Setting: A softly lit, upscale restaurant in the heart of the city. Candles flicker on the table between JULIA and THOMAS. They sit across from one another, sipping wine. The clink of silverware and low murmur of conversation surround them like a warm fog.

JULIA (smiling, lifting her glass)
To new beginnings.

THOMAS (raising his glass in return)
To moving forward.

Their glasses meet with a gentle chime. Julia takes a sip, her eyes never leaving Thomas. She notes the slight tremble in his hand as he sets his glass down.

JULIA
It’s been... too long since we caught up like this. I missed it.

She says it warmly, but her mind is elsewhere. She watches every microexpression for a tell.

If he knows, he’ll show it. He always had a terrible poker face.

THOMAS (nodding)
Yeah. Life gets in the way, doesn’t it? But I’m glad we’re doing this. You look—well. Really well.

He keeps his tone even, his smile effortless. But inside, a tight coil winds in his chest.

She doesn’t know. She can’t know. Not yet. Not until I’m ready to disappear.

JULIA (laughs lightly)
You always were a terrible liar, Thomas. I know I look tired.

THOMAS
Not tired. Just... thoughtful.

He leans forward slightly, careful not to overplay his concern. A practiced move—he’s had time to rehearse.

JULIA
Things at work have been demanding. But I’m working on something... big. You know how it goes.

She keeps her voice casual, but there’s a glint in her eye. She watches to see if he flinches.

I shouldn’t have said that. Too much. He might connect the dots. But if he does… maybe that’s not the worst thing.

THOMAS (tilting his head)
Still at the firm?

JULIA
Mm-hmm. Still chasing ghosts and secrets.

A pause. Their eyes meet. Silence stretches just a fraction too long.

THOMAS (breaking it with a laugh)
Some things never change.

He cuts into his steak, chewing slowly. He feels her gaze still on him. He doesn’t like it. He’s used to being watched, but not by her—not like this.

If she knew what I was planning… would she stop me? Or join me?

JULIA
And you? Still consulting? Traveling?

THOMAS (nods)
Here and there. I’ve got a few things in the works. Nothing concrete.

He lies smoothly. The tickets are already booked. The safe house in Lisbon is ready. Just one more week.

She can’t follow. I won’t let her.

JULIA (softly)
You always said you’d leave someday. I never thought you meant it.

Thomas looks up, eyes flickering.

THOMAS
I never thought I did, either. But sometimes the ground shifts under you, and you’ve got to move or be buried.

Julia smiles, but the corners of her mouth are tight.

He’s going to run. I know that now. And he doesn’t know I’m the one who set the trap he’s trying to escape.

JULIA (gently)
Be careful, Thomas. The world isn’t as forgiving as it once was.

THOMAS
Neither are old friends.

A beat. They both sip their wine, the candle between them flickering as if uncertain which way the air is moving.

Outside, the city hums, indifferent. Inside, two people share a meal—two ghosts, smiling through secrets, waiting for the first mask to fall.

plain.html:
Sure! Here's a scene where the two characters engage in polite conversation at dinner while their internal subtext carries the tension of their conflicting secrets:

Setting: A cozy Italian restaurant with dim lighting and soft jazz playing in the background. The table is set with flickering candles and plates of pasta. Claire and Mark sit across from each other, their smiles warm on the surface but carrying an underlying tension.

Claire: (lifting her glass of red wine and smiling) "Cheers, to new beginnings."
(I can't believe he's sitting here so calmly. Does he know? He can't know. God, if he finds out...)

Mark: (raising his glass to meet hers) "To new beginnings."
(New beginnings, huh? Fitting words coming from someone lying through her teeth. She doesn't suspect me—yet. But I have to be careful tonight. Keep it light, like nothing's wrong.)

Claire: (twirling her fork in her spaghetti) "So, how's work been this week? Still as relentless as usual?"
(Keep it casual. Just keep talking. If I steer the conversation away from anything personal, he won't have a reason to ask questions...)

Mark: (forcing a small chuckle) "It’s been busy, but you know, nothing I can’t handle. How about you? Any interesting projects lately?"
(She’s deflecting. Classic Claire. But why? If I push her too hard, she’ll get suspicious. Stay patient. I’ll learn what I need without her even realizing.)

Claire: (nodding quickly) "Oh, you know, the usual grant applications and research proposals. Same old, same old. I'm trying to keep things balanced, though—it’s important not to get too wrapped up in the chaos."
(Balanced. What a joke. Like I have any balance left after what I did. But he doesn't seem to be piecing it together... yet. Just smile. Always smile.)

Mark: (leaning back slightly) "That’s a good mindset. I admire that about you—how grounded you always seem, no matter what’s going on."
(Grounded? If only she knew I’ve been digging into all the 'grounded' little details she’s been hiding. I just need one slip, one crack. Come on, Claire, give me something to work with.)

Claire: (smiling tightly) "Well, we all have our secrets. Don't we?" (laughs lightly)
(Did I just say that? Stupid! Why would I say that? Just play it off, make it seem innocent... He’s looking at me too closely.)

Mark: (briefly holding her gaze, then smiling) "True enough. But you’ve always been good at keeping things in order. Some secrets are better kept that way."
(Did she just flinch? Interesting. What kind of secrets does she think she’s hiding from me? I need to tread carefully; she’s sharper than she lets on.)

Claire: (quickly switching the subject) "This cabernet is excellent. Where do you think they source their wine? Napa, maybe?"
(Perfect. Divert him. Keep the evening pleasant. If he pushes too much, the cracks will show. And I can’t... I can’t let him see through me.)

Mark: (taking a sip of his own wine) "Could be. It has that kind of richness Napa wines are known for."
(She’s running. Avoiding. The way she shifts topics so swiftly—it’s almost impressive. Not that it matters. By the end of the night, I’ll have what I need. Let her think she’s in control for now.)

Claire: (glancing at the candle’s flame, her tone softening) "You know, it’s nice to slow down like this. We should do it more often."
(Am I saying too much? He has no idea what I’ve done—or why I had to do it. I just have to get through tonight without slipping up.)

Mark: (giving her a small smile) "I agree. Life’s too short not to... enjoy the moments that matter."
(Enjoy this moment while you can, Claire. It’s the calm before the storm. Once I have proof, this little act of yours will all come crashing down.)

Narration: The waiter approaches their table to check if they need anything else. Both Claire and Mark smile warmly at him, momentarily united in politeness yet utterly divided beneath their calm facades. The secrets they guard weigh heavy, hidden just beneath the surface like a storm waiting to break.

Certainly! Here's the scene:

Scene: A cozy Italian restaurant, softly lit with flickering candlelight. Two colleagues, Emily and Daniel, sit across from each other at a small round table, the air alive with the smell of fresh basil and garlic. Their smiles are warm, but there's a tension in their eyes as they scan the menu and sip from their glasses of red wine.

Emily: [Setting down her glass] “This place is lovely, Daniel. Great choice. Do you come here often?”

Her words are light, effortless, but her stomach twists. Did he already figure it out? She hopes not. She just needs to get through this meal without letting on—without betraying that the promotion he's been working toward is already hers.

Daniel: [Glancing up with a soft smile] “Not too often, but it’s a favorite. You looked like you might appreciate something cozy after this week.”
He’s practiced this calm tone. Stay relaxed. Don’t give her a reason to suspect anything. She’s sharp, though. Maybe sharper than he thought. Does she know what he found out about her little oversight in the quarterly report?

Emily: [Laughing lightly] “You’re right, it’s been a week. I barely had time to breathe, let alone cook. Thank you for organizing this.”

Play to his ego, she reminds herself. Keep Daniel engaged and comfortable. If he confronts her directly about the promotion—or worse, if he asks what she knows—she’s going to have to scramble.

Daniel: [Cutting into his chicken parmesan] “Of course. It’s nice to take a break from everything, isn’t it? Work has been... intense lately.”
Careful. Don’t push too hard. Let it simmer. But why is she so composed? Maybe she really is oblivious. Or maybe she's just that good. Either way, he has the email proof of her error in his back pocket, and when the time is right...

Emily: [Nodding thoughtfully] “Intense is a good word for it. But I think we’ve been managing well, don’t you?”

She forces herself to meet his gaze when he looks up from his plate. Does he know? Has he already figured out that she pitched her idea during that impromptu meeting with their boss last week? It wasn’t exactly teamwork, but her career was at stake.

Daniel: [Pausing, then smiling easily] “I’d say so. We make a good team.”
On the surface, a harmless compliment. Underneath, a test. He watches her reaction closely. Her smile doesn’t falter; he’ll give her that. But does she really think she can outmaneuver him long-term? He’ll let her slip up first.

Emily: [Leaning back in her chair, gesturing to the waiter] “More wine?”

If she can keep this light and pleasant, maybe he won’t probe further. Maybe she can avoid an argument—not that she owes him an explanation. She worked for that promotion fair and square. Mostly.

Daniel: [Shrugging lightly, holding up his glass] “Sure, why not? It’s the perfect evening for it.”
It’s almost impressive, how she can look so composed. But he’s seen the cracks before. He just has to wait for one more. Then he’ll have her—and a very interesting conversation with the higher-ups.

Emily: [Lifting her glass as the waiter pours] “To all the hard work finally paying off.”
Her tone is impossibly steady, but her pulse races. The toast was a gamble, but if she plays it right, it might throw him off the scent... or at least buy her time to secure the deal.

Daniel: [Clinking her glass lightly with his own] “To success.”
She thinks this is over. But it’s nowhere near over.

The two smile at each other across the flickering candle, both outwardly calm, but beneath their polite façades, the war has already begun.

instruction.html:
Scene: A Dimly Lit Bistro

The restaurant buzzes softly with the hum of conversation and the clink of silverware. At a small table near a candle sputtering in its glass, Evelyn straightens her napkin, her movements precise. Across from her, Peter, his tie slightly loosened, swirls the wine in his glass with an absentminded focus.

Evelyn: (smiling too brightly) “You always pick the nicest places. How do you find them? I mean, I’ve lived in this city longer than you, but somehow you always surprise me.”

I know what you’ve done, Peter. I’m not letting you see me flinch. Not tonight.

Peter: (a small shrug) “I don’t know, I kind of just stumble across them. It’s intuition, I guess. Or dumb luck.” (He takes a sip of wine, meeting her eyes briefly.) “But this place... yeah, it seemed like your kind of vibe.”

She’s testing me again. That smile—God, it’s too sharp tonight. She knows something, doesn’t she? Keep it steady. Keep it light.

Evelyn: “Well, it’s a perfect choice. Cozy, but not too stuffy. And this wine—” (she raises her glass, letting the candlelight catch the ruby liquid) “—is excellent. You really do have great taste.”

In restaurants, maybe. In people? Questionable. Let’s see how long you can keep pretending.

Peter: (leaning back slightly, feigning ease) “Oh, you know me. A man of simple pleasures. A good meal, good company... it doesn’t take much.”

Don’t look at her hand. Don’t look at her hand. Has she taken it off yet? No... it’s still there. Jesus.

Evelyn: (tilting her head, her earrings glint) “Simple pleasures, huh? That’s funny... I would’ve pegged you as more ambitious than that. Am I wrong?”

Say something, Peter. Admit it. Say it aloud. Don’t make me drag it out of you.

Peter: (laughing softly, a touch hollow) “I prefer to save my ambition for the office. Outside of that, life’s short. You’ve gotta enjoy it where you can, right?”

Change the subject, keep moving, keep moving. She’s watching me too closely. Damn it, does she really know? Or is she just fishing?

Evelyn: (nodding thoughtfully, her tone warm but her gaze sharp) “That’s true. Life does have a way of sneaking up on you when you’re busy with... other things.”

Like lies. Like the affair you keep telling yourself you’ve hidden perfectly. I wonder if she calls you ‘darling’ the same way I do.

Peter: (pausing, then chuckling as if nothing’s amiss) “Doesn’t it, though? One moment you think you’ve got all the time in the world, and the next—bam. Everything’s different.”

Like discovering the engagement ring in your drawer, Evelyn. That wasn’t for me, was it?

Evelyn: (smiling sweetly, setting her glass down with a soft clink) “Exactly. Things can change so suddenly. Like flipping a switch.”

I could confront you right now, in front of all these strangers. I could. But I want to see how far you’ll carry this charade.

Peter: (leaning forward slightly, his elbows resting lightly on the table) “But sometimes those changes turn out to be... for the better. Don’t you think?”

Maybe it’s not too late. Maybe she hasn’t guessed. I can fix this. I have to fix this before—

Evelyn: (leaning in to mirror him, her voice dropping ever so slightly) “Oh, absolutely. Change can be... liberating. When you let it.”

You didn’t fix anything, Peter. The truth always bubbles up, eventually. Just like it did with me.

The waiter appears then, two plates balanced effortlessly in his hands. Evelyn and Peter both snap back into themselves, their polite masks sliding more firmly into place as their dishes are served. The waiter leaves, and for a long moment, neither of them speaks.

Then Evelyn picks up her fork and knife, slicing elegantly into her food. She glances up, catching Peter’s gaze.

Evelyn: (brightly) “Shall we toast? To changes.”

Peter: (hesitating, then lifting his glass) “To changes.”

And to destruction, Evelyn thinks, as she takes a slow, deliberate sip.

And to survival, Peter thinks, as he drains his glass.

Scene: A Quiet Italian Bistro

The warm glow of candlelight flickers between them. Plates of fettuccine sit untouched, the waiter long gone. A string quartet hums softly in the corner, their violins threading through moments of silence like a needle through cloth. Across the table, Eleanor smiles. Mark returns it.

They are careful not to look at their hands.

Eleanor: "Have you always been a red wine person?" (What are we doing here, Mark?)

Mark: (Smile. Keep it steady, even. Don't give anything away.) "I guess I have. Not a beer guy, really." (She's searching my face already. Stop gripping the glass so hard, Mark.) "What about you?"

Eleanor: (What about me? Mark, what do you know?) "Oh, white wine only. You know that." (That’s it. Keep it light. He doesn’t know. He can’t. Not if I’m careful.) "Too many headaches with red."

Mark: (Right. A headache. Okay. Stay in this moment. Just stay here – don’t think about – don’t think about where you were last night, don’t–) "Yeah, you’ve said that. Something about tannins, right?" (What horrible, trivial things we say when we can’t tell each other the truth.)

Eleanor: (Tannins. Tannins. I’m ripping apart inside, and here we are, talking about tannins. God.) "Exactly. Good memory." (I sound natural, don’t I? God, I sound natural, right? Breathe, Eleanor. Smile again. Keep him with you.) "You’ve been distracted all night. Are you okay?" (Too much? Too probing? Reel it back…)

Mark: (Shit. Caught. Is she suspicious? No. No, she can’t be. There’s no way she could know.) "Work stuff, I think. Just... a heavy week." (That’s even true, isn’t it? Except not in the way she thinks. No details, Mark. Keep it vague.) "I’d rather talk about you, though. How’s the new apartment?"

Eleanor: *(The apartment? The one where I…? Mark, how much do you want me to admit?) "Oh, it’s small but cozy." (And three blocks from Anthony’s place. God, I should never have moved so close. Should I even say his name aloud right now?) "I like the big windows." (Do I? I don’t even notice them anymore. I’m never home long enough.)

Mark: (Small but cozy. Sure. Except I saw someone leaving her building. Last night. Who was he?) "That’s great. Always nice to have natural light." (Was it him? It had to be him. I’ll just ask later. Not now. Not here. Just… keep calm.)

Eleanor: (Natural light? Is that a metaphor? God, maybe I’m inventing his tension entirely. Maybe he knows nothing. He’s not asking, he’s not accusing. This is fine. We’re fine. Keep breathing.) "I know, right? How’s your place holding up? Still… uh, minimalistic?" (Why do I sound like I’m choking? He barely takes anything out of me and I unravel. This guilt is eating me alive.)

Mark: (Minimalistic. Is that her way of reminding me how empty it is without her there? Is that her hint, or am I reading into everything now?) "Still pretty stark, yeah." (I cleaned for hours this morning. Bleached everything. Scrubbed. Tried to erase... God, stop thinking about it. She doesn't know. She can't. You were so careful.) "Maybe I should hire a decorator or something."

Eleanor: (His voice just cracked. Barely. Would anyone else have caught it but me? Maybe he is hiding something, too? Oh no. What if he–? No. No, don’t spiral now. Just… answer the man, Eleanor.) "You should. You’d be surprised what some throw pillows could do." (Throw pillows? Jesus, I’m losing it. Keep laughing. Keep pretending. Keep everyone from seeing so much.)

Mark: (Throw pillows. She’s laughing. She doesn’t know. How could she know? Be grateful, Mark. Grateful for her laugh, her lightness. Hold on to that.) "Yeah, maybe." (Throw pillows aren’t going to fix what I did last night. Nothing will fix it. But she doesn’t know.)

Eleanor: (Do I know him anymore? Does he know me? Are we just two strangers wearing the memory of trust like an old coat? I hate this. I hate myself.) "Well, if you need help picking colors, I’m your girl." (Make it sound true. Make it sound like you’ll still be here. Like you’ll still be us when this secret between us cracks open, the way secrets always do.)

Mark: *(I don’t deserve you. I don’t deserve your light or your voice. I don’t deserve this meal. But I can’t stop sitting here like some fool trying to hold on to something that’s already gone. Do you feel it, too?) "I’ll keep that in mind. Thanks." (And I love you. And I hate myself. And I love you. And what happens when you find out?)

Their forks clink against porcelain as they both pretend to eat. Neither has taken a bite.

plain.html:
Title: Beneath the Surface

Setting: A cozy, upscale restaurant with dim lighting and soft music playing in the background. The table is elegantly set, and a flickering candle adds a warm glow.

Characters:

  • Emma: A poised marketing executive. She’s dressed smartly, projecting confidence—but inside, she's masking a significant personal dilemma.
  • David: An affable accountant. His demeanor is relaxed, but beneath his calm exterior, he's wrestling with a professional crisis.

Scene begins with Emma and David seated at a small, round table. They're midway through their meal.

Emma: (smiling warmly) This place is fantastic, David. How did you find it?

David: (glancing around appreciatively) Oh, a colleague mentioned it. Said the steak was to die for. I'm glad you're enjoying it.

Subtext (David): I need to steer this conversation away from work. If she finds out about the audit, everything could unravel.

Emma: The ambiance is perfect. Feels like the kind of place where you could just... forget about everything for a while.

Subtext (Emma): Perfect to pretend, just for tonight, that everything’s alright—that I’m not about to make a life-altering decision behind your back.

David: Absolutely. It’s nice to escape. Let’s toast to a well-deserved break. (raises glass)

Emma: To tranquility amidst the chaos. (taps her glass gently against his)

Subtext (David): Tranquility—what a concept. If the firm knew I covered those numbers... I need a plan.

Emma: (taking a sip, setting the glass down) So, how’s work going? Any exciting projects?

Subtext (Emma): If only he could just tell me. Then maybe… we could find a way out together.

David: Work is... steady. You know how it is. Lots of numbers. (light chuckle) But what about you? Any new campaigns on the horizon?

Subtext (David): Steady as a ship about to sink. I need to sound convincing. When did lying become second nature?

Emma: Oh, the usual. Balancing creativity and reality. There's always something in the pipeline.

Subtext (Emma): So many plans. All reliant on a truth I haven’t shared with you yet.

David: (nods knowingly) That’s life, isn't it? Always a balancing act.

Subtext (David): Balancing what I know and what I can never admit. But I’m running out of time.

Emma: (leans in slightly) Sometimes I wonder if it's all worth it.

Subtext (Emma): Will you still be there when the truth comes out?

David: (looking into her eyes) Oh, I think so. Life has a way of working out, doesn't it?

Subtext (David): Please let this be true. If only I could believe it myself.

Emma: (softly, with sincerity) I hope so, David. I really hope so.

Subtext (Emma): I need to believe you’re right—just this once.

The scene ends with both Emma and David lingering in the moment, their secrets hovering in the silence between their words, each drawing comfort from the other's presence, while the weight of what remains unspoken continues to hang over them.

Title: Secrets at Supper

Setting: A cozy, dimly lit restaurant with soft violin music playing in the background.

Characters:

  • Emma: A composed woman in her mid-30s, wearing a smart, navy blue dress.
  • Robert: A charming man in his late 30s, in a well-tailored suit.

Scene:

Emma and Robert are seated at a corner table, a candle flickering gently between them. Their plates are elegantly presented with gourmet dishes. Emma lifts her glass of red wine, her smile polished and controlled.

Emma: (Lifting her glass.) To old friends and new adventures, Robert.

Robert: (Clinking his glass against hers.) To new adventures, indeed. You've always had a knack for making life sound exciting.

(As Emma takes a sip, she mentally braces herself, hoping Robert hasn’t heard the rumor about her sudden departure from her last job. Her heart beats faster at the thought.)

Emma: (Setting her glass down, looking at her plate.) So, how have things been at the firm? Last I heard, you were up for a big promotion.

Robert: Oh, you know how it is. Lots of late nights and early mornings. The promotion is still a work in progress.

(Robert's mind races. It's not just the promotion; he plans to start his own venture soon. Acquiring the right contacts—like Emma—is crucial. He needs her unaware of his immediate plans.)

Emma: It sounds intense but rewarding! I’m sure they see your value.

(Emma's thoughts drift to the letters of reference she stole from Robert’s boss. She’d rather he not know she’d approached them for insights in her ongoing job hunt.)

Robert: (Cutting into his steak, maintaining eye contact.) Well, one never truly knows, does one? But you—I heard you’ve been traveling quite a bit lately. Anywhere intriguing?

(Emma forces a casual laugh, concealing her anxiety about her recent “off-the-grid” trip to secure a position at an overseas competitor of Robert’s company.)

Emma: Just some personal exploration, nothing too exotic. But I've always found travel to be enlightening, don’t you agree?

Robert: Definitely. Travel opens the mind. It provides a fresh perspective on one's... situation.

(He hopes she doesn’t suspect his recent travels have been in pursuit of potential investors for his new business idea.)

Emma: (Picking at her salad, carefully.) Perspective is key, isn’t it? Always good to keep options open and see where life leads you.

(Emma wonders if she should broach the subject of potential collaborations without revealing too much. She needs his expertise but can't risk him suspecting her motives.)

Robert: True, it’s always advantageous to keep an open mind. Speaking of which, have you considered any... collaborative opportunities recently?

(Robert leans forward slightly, looking for a hint of interest in her eyes while praying she hasn't discovered his meetings with competitors.)

Emma: Oh, I do love collaboration. You never know what could come from pooling talents.

(She smiles brightly, masking her relief. His inquiry felt genuine rather than probing.)

Robert: Ah, that’s the spirit I like to hear. Maybe we should brainstorm sometime. Talents like ours could surely conjure something remarkable.

(Robert silently wonders how far she’d go to protect her own interests if the truth came out.)

Emma: That sounds promising. I’d like that very much.

(Her mind is already formulating a plan to work with Robert, hoping to keep her connection to his competition under wraps for the time being.)

They return to eating, engaging in small talk, both keenly aware of the unspoken tension simmering beneath polite smiles and well-rehearsed replies.

The candle flickers uncertainly between them, much like their mutual trust.

instruction.html:
The clinking of dinnerware and the gentle murmur of voices formed a cozy cocoon in Il Forno, a favorite little Italian restaurant nestled in the heart of the city. Sarah twirled fettuccine on her fork, suppressing the whirl of her thoughts. Across from her sat Alex, whose fingers tapped an idle rhythm against the tablecloth, unaware of the storm brewing behind her smile.

"This pasta is delightful," Sarah said, keeping her voice light. "The chef never disappoints here."

"Absolutely," Alex replied, his eyes briefly flicking to her before settling on his own plate. "I remember you mentioned once how much you love this place. Thought it would be nice to revisit."

He focused on each bite, though the taste seemed dulled today, overshadowed by the echo of last night's revelation. His gaze drifted to the ring hidden in his pocket, a decision he hadn't yet figured out how to unravel.

"It was a great choice," Sarah kept her smile steady, even as her mind danced around the confirmation email she’d read that morning—her transfer to London, set to begin in two weeks. A fresh start. Something neither had discussed, something she hadn't dared to disrupt their usual rhythm with.

"I hope we can do this more often," Alex ventured, forcing the tone of optimism into his words. He couldn't pinpoint whether it was the memory of their years together or the fear of what lay ahead that churned his stomach more.

"Yes, we should," Sarah nodded, warmth infused in her voice that she wished matched the certainty beneath it. "Dinner has always been our thing, hasn’t it?"

"Our way to pause the world," he replied, his voice softer. He tried to imagine the implications of a ring, of promises altered by truths still unspoken. How strange to be planning a future while tethered to secrets.

A moment of silence fell, an almost imperceptible crack in their practiced ease.

"So, how's work?" Alex asked, diverting the path as he speared a piece of chicken.

"Oh, the usual," Sarah replied, dismissing with a slight wave, careful not to let her eyes betray the concoction of excitement and terror she felt about the move. The promotion she had wanted, something she’d ensured Alex would support—if only he knew.

"Busy as usual here, too," he mirrored her deflection, thoughts snapping to the moment he’d learned of a merger that would mean uprooting—or worse—a harsh blow to everything he'd promised her.

They continued, weaving words that lingered in the air like paper butterflies, each hiding the delicate origami folds of truths left unsaid. The dessert menu arrived, a sweet distraction, though it offered no resolve, just a prelude to the evening's lingering farewells.

Every shared glance held volumes left unvoiced, and while the conversation enveloped them, the understanding that soon, they'd need to unravel these hidden knots glinted briefly in their eyes, before both looked away.

Scene: A Cozy Bistro, Evening

Characters: Sarah and Mark

The bistro hums softly with the evening chatter of diners and the clink of cutlery. A candle flickers between Sarah and Mark, casting gentle shadows on their faces. They sit across from each other, a half-finished bottle of red wine between them. Everything is perfectly arranged, yet there's a tension in the air thick enough to slice with a dull knife.

Sarah: (smiling lightly as she twirls pasta around her fork) The linguine here is always so good. You were right about this place.

Internal - Sarah: I can’t believe I’m sitting here like everything is normal. How can I ever tell him?

Mark: (nodding, matching her smile) Yeah, it's one of my favorites. I’m glad you like it. He pauses, looking at her intently. I’ve always thought you had a great taste in food.

Internal - Mark: I should just tell her. Tonight. But what if it ruins everything?

Sarah: (meets his gaze, her heart skipping, trying to maintain her smile) Thanks, Mark. That means a lot coming from you. She takes a sip of wine, thinking of how to keep the evening’s facade steady.

Internal - Sarah: Does he know? God, I hope not. If he finds out from someone else, it’ll be the end of us.

Mark: (leans back in his chair, picking at the edge of the tablecloth) So, how's work been treating you lately? Still keeping you busy?

Internal - Mark: If she asks me about work, I don't think I can keep pretending. Why did I even agree to this dinner?

Sarah: (sighs, placing her fork down delicately) Always busy, but it's good. Keeps me out of trouble. She laughs softly, though her eyes dart briefly to the window as if searching for escape.

Internal - Sarah: Just keep the conversation light. He mustn't suspect.

Mark: (chuckles, fighting a twinge of guilt) Trouble doesn't seem your style. Not out of character, but surprising nonetheless.

Internal - Mark: I wish she could see how much I’m tangled in my own mess. But this secret—it could change everything.

Sarah: (reaches across the table, brushing his hand lightly) We all have our secrets, don’t we?

Internal - Sarah: Please tell me yours doesn’t clash with mine. Please, let it be anything other than that.

Mark: (staring at her hand, his heart racing) Yeah, I guess some are better left unsaid.

Internal - Mark: I can’t lose her over this. Not now. Not ever.

They each lift their glasses, a silent toast to the unspoken truths resting heavily in the spaces between their words. The candle flickers once more, casting their secrets into a dance of shadows on the wall.
